articles.title: NASA Science Data Powers New Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars
articles.summary: Open data from NASA’s Fermi mission helped an international team of scientists develop a method for finding pulsars about a million times faster than before.
articles.content:
NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, illustrated here, scans the entire sky every three hours as it orbits Earth. Its publicly available data helps scientists find the rapidly spinning cores of dead stars, known as pulsars. NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center/Chris Smith (USRA/GESTAR)

An international team of scientists has developed a method that can find pulsars in publicly available NASA data about a million times faster than before. This opens the door to discovering many more of these rapidly spinning objects. A paper describing the results published Thursday in the Physical Review Letters.

Using 15 years of data from NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope and a cryptography-based method developed by study co-authors Dotan Gazith and Barak Zackay from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, the team found PSR J1622−7204, an isolated pulsar spinning 261 times per second, using the equivalent of 10 hours of computing time on a standard computer processor.

By comparison, the previous best method failed to find the pulsar, despite using enough computing power that a standard processor would take 600 years to perform the calculation.

A pulsar is a rapidly spinning neutron star that sweeps beams of radiation toward Earth, much like a lighthouse. Finding pulsars in gamma-ray data is extraordinarily difficult because Fermi detects only a tiny number of photons from a given pulsar, mixed in with background noise from other gamma-ray-emitting sources and the broader universe. To find the signal, researchers must accurately guess several unknowns at once: how fast the star spins, how quickly the spin is slowing down, and precisely where it sits in the sky. Searching every possible combination would require an impossible number of computations.

"We don't see every rotation from the pulsar, and we can't just count the rotations to work out where the photon came from," said lead author Daniel Pook-Kolb, a scientist at the Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics (Albert Einstein Institute) in Germany. “We have a four-dimensional grid, and we must search each direction with millions of trials in it. There’s just not enough computing power on Earth to do it.”

This artist's concept shows a pulsar, which emits light in regular pulses as it rotates, like a cosmic lighthouse. Pulsars are dense remnants of exploded stars, and are part of a class of objects called neutron stars. Openly available data from NASA's Fermi space telescope can help scientists spot pulsars in the gamma-ray spectrum. NASA/JPL-Caltech

Traditionally, scientists have searched for these pulsars by breaking Fermi data into smaller chunks and analyzing them by crowdsourcing computing power from volunteers around the world. Even with these volunteers contributing their computers’ unused processing power to run searches, it typically took the equivalent of hundreds of computer-years to identify a single pulsar.

Gazith and Zackay realized that the search could be transformed into a geometry problem: finding the shortest vector in a high-dimensional lattice, or a regularly spaced array of points. This lattice technique draws on algorithms developed by cryptographers trying to break encryption systems designed to resist code-breaking by future quantum computers. The method has also been used to help make satellite navigation systems more efficient.

"We have nothing to do with cryptography in our analysis here, but those algorithms can help us solve the problem of searching for pulsars in our data," Gazith said.

Each trial run of the algorithm took about five minutes on a single computer core — easily doable on a standard laptop, which usually has between two and eight cores. Once the lattice method identified a pulsar candidate, the researchers confirmed it by feeding in the full Fermi data set, revealing a signal so strong it could not be a chance occurrence.

The team’s next goal is even more ambitious: finding pulsars in binary systems, where a pulsar orbits a star. These discoveries have long been considered out of reach because a companion star’s gravity distorts the signal in ways that have made these pulsars essentially impossible to discover with traditional methods.

"We know that there are probably tens or maybe even hundreds of these pulsars in the data set that we just couldn't find," said Colin Clark, an astrophysicist at the Max Planck Institute who co-authored the study. "The next goal is to extend the searches and use the combination of the new algorithm and the crowdsourced computing power from volunteers in our Einstein@Home program to hopefully find many new pulsars that we think should be there.”

This view of the gamma-ray sky is constructed from one year of Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) observations. The map shows the rate at which the LAT instrument detects gamma rays with energies above 300 million electron volts — about 120 million times the energy of visible light — from different sky directions. Brighter colors equal higher rates. Fermi's openly available data archive contains a wealth of information that has supercharged scientific studies about the extreme universe. NASA/DOE/Fermi LAT Collaboration

The discovery would not have happened without NASA's longstanding, Gold Standard Science policy of making its science data, including data from Fermi, freely available to anyone. Launched in 2008, Fermi surveys the entire sky every three hours, observing the universe in gamma rays — the highest-energy form of light. After an initial one-year calibration period, all Fermi data became fully public and continues to be released as soon as it is processed.

"The nice thing about NASA data is it's all open," Clark said. "All 18 years of Fermi data have been made public, and the data just keeps growing."

That openness allowed researchers from outside the Fermi mission, including the cryptography-inspired team, to apply a completely new approach to the dataset. NASA’s support for the science community, through open software and tools such as NASA's Fermitools, enabled the team to prepare their dataset before beginning their analysis.

The Fermi mission has grown its catalog from a few hundred gamma ray sources to thousands, with new findings emerging as scientists apply fresh ideas to the same data.

"Any search that one team is doing, another team can just go and do that and check the search," said Elizabeth Hays, Fermi project scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. "It's made all of the science better."

For more information about NASA's Fermi mission, visit:

https://www.nasa.gov/fermi

By Amanda Moon Adams

Communications Lead for the Office of the Chief Science Data Officer

articles.personality_title: New method finds pulsars a million times faster using NASA’s open data

Pulsars are rapidly spinning neutron stars that send beams of radiation toward Earth, but finding them in this data is very hard because their signals are faint and mixed with background noise.

The new technique treats the search like a geometry problem, making it much faster and easier.

**Impact** – This discovery shows that scientists can now find pulsars much more quickly and with less computing power. It opens the possibility to find many more pulsars hidden in the data, including those in complex systems where pulsars orbit other stars, which were previously too hard to detect.

articles.title: The BepiColombo spacecraft is finally entering orbit around Mercury
articles.summary: After an eight-year voyage towards the sun, the BepiColombo spacecraft can finally begin its mission to unpick the many mysteries of our solar system's smallest planet
articles.content:
After an eight-year voyage towards the sun, the BepiColombo spacecraft can finally begin its mission to unpick the many mysteries of our solar system's smallest planet

Artist’s impression of BepiColombo orbiting Mercury ESA/ATG medialab

After a long and ponderous journey, the BepiColombo spacecraft will finally enter Mercury’s orbit on 21 November. Over the course of the next year, it will investigate the planet’s geology, its tenuous atmosphere and its magnetic field in an effort to understand how it formed and evolved over time.

BepiColombo, a joint mission of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), launched in October 2018. Mercury’s proximity to the sun makes it incredibly difficult to reach without overshooting the planet and falling into the sun, so the spacecraft had to take a long and looping path over the past eight years, flying past both Venus and Mercury several times and using their gravity to make subtle tweaks to its trajectory. In 2024, an issue with the thrusters lengthened that journey even further, pushing the arrival date back from 2025 to 2026. Now, it has finally arrived.

While it is arriving at Mercury as a single spacecraft, BepiColombo actually comprises two separate orbiters: ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO, or Mio). In December, the two will split apart and move to different orbits – MPO on a near-circular path that takes 2.3 hours to complete an orbit, and Mio on a more distant elliptical orbit, where it will take 9.3 hours to circle Mercury.

Advertisement

Those split orbits complement the differing scientific objectives of the two spacecraft. MPO is more than twice the size of MMO, and its 11 scientific instruments focus largely on studying Mercury itself. Its instruments include several types of spectrometer to measure the makeup of the surface, a laser altimeter to map its terrain and instruments to study the makeup of Mercury’s extremely thin atmosphere, called an exosphere.

Mio’s more distant orbit will allow it to study a broader area around Mercury. It has five sets of scientific instruments to study the magnetic field and atmosphere of the planet, as well as the solar wind that blows strongly in the area close to the sun.

Free newsletter Sign up to Launchpad Sign up to newsletter

Now that the BepiColombo spacecraft are entering orbit, their primary mission is expected to last only one Earth year, which is a little more than four Mercury years. The mission could potentially be extended for another year, but beyond that the combination of limited fuel and extreme temperatures will make it all but impossible to keep going.

Over the course of the year, researchers hope that BepiColombo will provide enough data to solve some of Mercury’s many mysteries. Mercury’s magnetic field is bewildering, because it originates 400 kilometres above the planet’s centre and should have faded away long ago. Its atmosphere must be continuously supplied with material from the surface, but we are unsure exactly how that occurs. And its enormous iron core, much bigger proportionally than the core of any other planet in the solar system, makes its very formation and evolution a puzzle. If all goes well, BepiColombo will start to unravel the convoluted tale of our solar system’s smallest planet.
articles.reasoning: The article reports the successful arrival of the BepiColombo spacecraft at Mercury after an eight-year journey, marking a significant milestone in space exploration. This mission, a collaboration between ESA and JAXA, aims to provide valuable scientific data about Mercury's geology, atmosphere, and magnetic field, potentially solving longstanding planetary mysteries. The story has broad significance for humanity's understanding of the solar system and is detailed and focused on this major scientific achievement.
articles.personality_title: BepiColombo spacecraft begins orbit around Mercury after eight years
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Mercury is the smallest planet in our solar system and is very close to the sun. Because of this closeness, it is hard for spacecraft to reach it without being pulled into the sun. Scientists want to learn more about Mercury’s surface, thin atmosphere, and strange magnetic field.

**What happened** – On November 21, the BepiColombo spacecraft finally entered orbit around Mercury after traveling for eight years. This mission is a joint effort between the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan’s space agency (JAXA). The spacecraft actually consists of two parts: the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) from ESA and the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO or Mio) from JAXA. In December, these two will separate and orbit Mercury in different paths to study the planet from different angles.

**Impact** – This mission is important because it will help scientists understand Mercury’s unusual features. For example, Mercury has a magnetic field that is strange because it starts far above the planet’s center and should not exist anymore. Its atmosphere is very thin and needs to be constantly refilled, but scientists don’t know how. Also, Mercury has a very large iron core compared to other planets, and this mission may help explain how the planet formed and changed over time.

**What's next step** – After entering orbit, BepiColombo will spend about one Earth year studying Mercury, which is a bit more than four Mercury years. The mission might be extended for another year if conditions allow. The data collected will be used by scientists to better understand Mercury’s mysteries and improve our knowledge of how planets form and change.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After a long journey, the BepiColombo spacecraft has started orbiting Mercury to study its unique features and help solve planetary mysteries.
articles.personality_title_fr: La sonde BepiColombo entre enfin en orbite autour de Mercure après huit ans
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Mercure est la plus petite planète de notre système solaire et se trouve très près du soleil. À cause de cette proximité, il est difficile pour une sonde d’y arriver sans être attirée par le soleil. Les scientifiques veulent en savoir plus sur la surface, l’atmosphère très fine et le champ magnétique étrange de Mercure.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le 21 novembre, la sonde BepiColombo est enfin entrée en orbite autour de Mercure après un voyage de huit ans. Cette mission est une collaboration entre l’Agence spatiale européenne (ESA) et l’agence spatiale japonaise (JAXA). La sonde est en réalité composée de deux parties : le Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) de l’ESA et le Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO ou Mio) de la JAXA. En décembre, ces deux parties se sépareront pour orbiter Mercure sur des trajectoires différentes et étudier la planète sous plusieurs angles.

**Impact** – Cette mission est importante car elle aidera les scientifiques à mieux comprendre les caractéristiques étranges de Mercure. Par exemple, Mercure possède un champ magnétique qui est surprenant car il commence loin au-dessus du centre de la planète et ne devrait plus exister. Son atmosphère est très mince et doit être constamment renouvelée, mais on ne sait pas comment. De plus, Mercure a un noyau de fer très grand comparé aux autres planètes, et cette mission pourrait aider à expliquer comment la planète s’est formée et a évolué.

**Prochaine étape** – Après son entrée en orbite, BepiColombo passera environ un an terrestre à étudier Mercure, ce qui correspond à un peu plus de quatre années mercuriennes. La mission pourrait être prolongée d’une année si les conditions le permettent. Les données recueillies aideront les scientifiques à mieux comprendre les mystères de Mercure et à améliorer nos connaissances sur la formation et l’évolution des planètes.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Après un long voyage, la sonde BepiColombo commence à orbiter Mercure pour étudier ses caractéristiques uniques et résoudre ses mystères planétaires.
articles.personality_title_es: La nave BepiColombo entra finalmente en órbita alrededor de Mercurio tras ocho años
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Mercurio es el planeta más pequeño de nuestro sistema solar y está muy cerca del sol. Por esta cercanía, es difícil que una nave espacial llegue sin ser atraída por el sol. Los científicos quieren aprender más sobre la superficie, la atmósfera muy fina y el extraño campo magnético de Mercurio.

**Qué pasó** – El 21 de noviembre, la nave BepiColombo entró finalmente en órbita alrededor de Mercurio después de un viaje de ocho años. Esta misión es un esfuerzo conjunto de la Agencia Espacial Europea (ESA) y la Agencia Japonesa de Exploración Aeroespacial (JAXA). La nave en realidad está formada por dos partes: el Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) de la ESA y el Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO o Mio) de JAXA. En diciembre, estas dos partes se separarán y seguirán órbitas diferentes para estudiar el planeta desde distintos puntos.

**Impacto** – Esta misión es importante porque ayudará a los científicos a entender las características extrañas de Mercurio. Por ejemplo, Mercurio tiene un campo magnético que es raro porque comienza muy arriba del centro del planeta y no debería existir. Su atmósfera es muy delgada y necesita renovarse constantemente, pero no se sabe cómo. Además, Mercurio tiene un núcleo de hierro muy grande comparado con otros planetas, y esta misión podría ayudar a explicar cómo se formó y cambió con el tiempo.

**Próximo paso** – Después de entrar en órbita, BepiColombo pasará alrededor de un año terrestre estudiando Mercurio, que es un poco más de cuatro años mercurianos. La misión podría extenderse por otro año si las condiciones lo permiten. Los datos recogidos ayudarán a los científicos a entender mejor los misterios de Mercurio y a mejorar nuestro conocimiento sobre cómo se forman y cambian los planetas.

**Resumen en una frase** – Tras un largo viaje, la nave BepiColombo comienza a orbitar Mercurio para estudiar sus características únicas y resolver sus misterios planetarios.
